difficultyReason: The stimulus presents a mix of quantitative data and a notable subgroup exception. The correct answer makes a hedged comparative inference that respects the qualification. Trap answers either drop the qualifier (too strong), reverse the direction, or introduce plausible but unsupported worldly claims about the exception subgroup.
stimulus: A survey of 2,400 urban households found that those with at least one member who commutes by bicycle report lower annual transportation costs, on average, than households in which all members commute by car. However, among households with annual incomes below $30,000, the pattern reverses: bicycle-commuting households in this income bracket report transportation costs roughly equal to, or in some cases higher than, those of car-commuting households in the same bracket. The survey also found that bicycle-commuting households at all income levels report purchasing more health and fitness products annually than car-commuting households at comparable income levels.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bicycle commuting reduces transportation costs for all households regardless of income level.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The transportation cost savings associated with bicycle commuting do not apply equally across all income groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low-income households would be better served financially by switching from bicycle commuting to car commuting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spending on health and fitness products is the primary reason bicycle-commuting households have higher overall expenses than car-commuting households.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urban households that commute by bicycle tend to have higher incomes than those that commute by car.

explanations.correct: The survey shows that, overall, bicycle commuters have lower transportation costs than car commuters, but this advantage disappears or reverses in the lowest income bracket. This directly and strongly supports the hedged claim that the cost savings associated with bicycle commuting do not apply equally across all income groups — a modest, well-anchored inference that respects both the general trend and the exception.
explanations.A: Too strong. This is the dominant trap. The stimulus explicitly states that the cost advantage reverses among households earning below $30,000, which contradicts the claim that bicycle commuting reduces transportation costs 'for all households regardless of income level.'
explanations.B: Correct. The general finding (lower costs for bicycle commuters) combined with the exception at lower incomes directly supports the claim that the savings are not uniform across income groups. The hedged, comparative phrasing matches what the data actually show.
explanations.C: Opposite direction / unsupported. The stimulus reports that low-income bicycle-commuting households have costs roughly equal to or higher than low-income car-commuting households, but it does not establish that switching to car commuting would reduce their costs — costs could simply be comparable. This overreads the data and implies a prescriptive conclusion the stimulus does not support.
explanations.D: Scope creep and mis-scoped. The stimulus says bicycle-commuting households spend more on health and fitness products, but it never identifies this as the 'primary reason' for any cost difference, nor does it establish that bicycle-commuting households have higher overall expenses across the board.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported. While the data could be consistent with this, the stimulus makes no direct comparison of income levels between bicycle- and car-commuting households. The survey reports cost patterns within income brackets, not the income distribution of commuting choices.
